prompt: Given ∀x.p(x), use the Fitch System to prove ∃x.p(x).
hint: Use Universal Elimination to get p(a) for an arbitrary object constant, then Existential Introduction.

prompt: Given ∀x.(r(x) ⇒ s(x)), and r(a), use the Fitch System to prove s(a).
hint: Eliminate the universal to get r(a) ⇒ s(a), then use Implication Elimination.

prompt: Given ∃x.p(x), use the Fitch System to prove ∃x.(p(x) ∨ q(x)).
hint: Use the existential pattern: assume p(c), get p(c) ∨ q(c), generalize, discharge.

prompt: Use the Fitch System to prove ∀x.(q(x) ⇒ q(x)).
hint: Proof by opening with a placeholder and using Implication Introduction.

prompt: Given ∀x.(p(x) ⇒ q(x)), ∃x.p(x), use the Fitch System to prove ∃x.q(x).
hint: EE the existential for a new placeholder, use UE on the universal with that placeholder, and then conclude by existential introduction.

prompt: Consider a language with just two object constants - jack and jill. Given ∀x.(loves(x,jack)), use the Fitch System to prove ∃x.(loves(jack,x) ∧ loves(jill,x)).
hint: With a finite domain, check each constant. Use the universal to get facts about both and combine with conjunction, then existentially introduce.

prompt: Given ∀x.(p(x) ⇒ (q(x) ∨ r(x))) and ∀x.(r(x) ⇒ q(x)), use the Fitch System to prove ∀x.(p(x) ⇒ q(x)).
hint: Instantiate the universals with a fresh placeholder, derive a disjunction, then use Disjunction Elimination with q(c) ⇒ q(c) and r(c) ⇒ q(c). Close with Implication Introduction and then generalize using Universal Introduction (placeholders must be arbitrary per the Chapter 10 UI guidance ).

prompt: Given ∃x.(p(x) ∧ ∀y.(p(y) ⇒ r(x,y))) and ∀y.p(y), use the Fitch System to prove ∀y.∃x.r(x,y).
hint: Follow the existential pattern: assume the existential’s scope for a fresh placeholder c, derive ∀y.∃x.r(x,y) inside using UE and EI, close by Implication Introduction and then use UI to generalize c; finally apply EE to discharge the original existential (see the pattern explained in Chapter 10’s example of EE usage  and the formal EE rule statement ).

prompt: Given ∀x.(p(x) ⇒ q(x)) and ¬∃x.q(x), use the Fitch System to prove ¬∃x.p(x).
hint: To prove a negation, build two separate subproofs to apply Negation Introduction: first derive ∃x.q(x) from ∃x.p(x) using the existential pattern (UE, IE, EI, UI, EE as in Chapter 10’s worked pattern ), and second derive ¬∃x.q(x) from ∃x.p(x) by reiterating the premise; then conclude ¬∃x.p(x) by NI.

prompt: Given ∀x.(p(x) ⇒ ∃y.(r(x,y) ∧ t(y))) and ∀x.∀y.((r(x,y) ∧ t(y)) ⇒ s(x)) and ∀x.(s(x) ⇒ u(x)) and ∀x.(u(x) ⇒ v(x)), use the Fitch System to prove ∀x.(p(x) ⇒ v(x)).
hint: Follow the chapter’s existential pattern: assume an instance of the existential’s scope for a fresh placeholder, derive a consequent that does not contain that placeholder free, close with Implication Introduction, generalize by Universal Introduction, and apply Existential Elimination; also respect that UI must generalize only truly arbitrary placeholders and that EE’s consequent cannot contain the eliminated variable free (see the worked existential pattern and UI discussion in Chapter 10  ).

prompt: Given ∀x.(p(x) ⇒ ∀y.(r(y) ⇒ s(x,y))) and ∃x.p(x) and ∃y.r(y) and ∀x.∀y.(s(x,y) ⇒ (t(x) ∧ u(y))), use the Fitch System to prove ∃x.∃y.(t(x) ∧ u(y)).
hint: Work inside a p(c)-subproof, and then inside an r(d)-subproof; derive s(c,d), push it through to t(c) ∧ u(d), and existentially generalize c and d in the right order so that the final consequent is independent of the eliminated variable when you apply EE. This is exactly the existential pattern emphasized in Chapter 10 (assume scope → derive target → II → UI → EE) and requires care with UI’s arbitrariness condition for placeholders  .

prompt: Consider a language with just two object constants - a and b. Given p(a) ⇒ q(a) and p(b) ⇒ q(b) and p(a) ∨ p(b) and ∀x.(q(x) ⇒ (r(a) ∧ r(b))), use the Fitch System to prove ∀x.r(x).
hint: Prove the same consequent from each disjunct (use Or Elimination), then extract r(a) and r(b) and close with Domain Closure over the fixed domain {a, b}. Remember DC applies only when every object constant has been instantiated, and that Or Elimination needs one implication per disjunct with a shared consequent  .

prompt: Given ∃x.∀y.(p(y) ⇒ ¬r(x,y)) and ∃y.p(y), use the Fitch System to prove ∃z.¬∀x.r(x,z).
hint: Use nested existential subproofs with fresh placeholders c and d. Inside them, prove ¬∀x.r(x,d) by building two separate implications from ∀x.r(x,d), one concluding r(c,d) and the other concluding ¬r(c,d). Existentially generalize d, then discharge each existential using Implication Introduction, Universal Introduction, and Existential Elimination, following Chapter 10’s pattern.

prompt: Given ¬∃x.∃y.(p(x,y) ∧ q(y)), use the Fitch System to prove ∀x.(∃y.p(x,y) ⇒ ¬∀z.q(z)).
hint: For an arbitrary placeholder c, assume ∃y.p(c,y), then assume p(c,d) for a fresh placeholder d. Build two separate implications with antecedent ∀z.q(z): one concludes the existential sentence forbidden by the premise, and the other concludes its negation. Apply Negation Introduction, then discharge the witness assumption using Chapter 10’s II–UI–EE pattern. Finally discharge the outer assumption and generalize c.

prompt: Use the Fitch System to prove (∃x.p(x) ∧ ∀x.q(x)) ⇒ ∃x.(p(x) ∧ q(x)).
hint: Assume the antecedent and extract its conjuncts. Follow Chapter 10’s existential pattern: assume p(c) for a fresh placeholder, instantiate the universal statement at c, and construct the existential conclusion. Discharge the witness assumption with II, UI, and EE before closing the outer subproof.

prompt: Given ∃x.∀y.p(x,y), use the Fitch System to prove ∃z.p(z,z).
hint: Use the chapter's existential pattern: assume ∀y.p(c,y) for a fresh placeholder c, instantiate at c, and introduce the existential goal. Then apply Implication Introduction, Universal Introduction, and Existential Elimination.

prompt: Given ∃x.∀y.p(x,y) and ∀x.∀y.(p(x,y) ⇒ p(y,x)), use the Fitch System to prove ∃z.∀y.(p(z,y) ∧ p(y,z)).
hint: Assume ∀y.p(c,y) for a fresh placeholder c. For an arbitrary d, derive both p(c,d) and p(d,c), then generalize d and existentially generalize c. Finish with the chapter’s Implication Introduction, Universal Introduction, and Existential Elimination pattern.

prompt: Given ¬∃x.(p(x) ∧ q(x)), use the Fitch System to prove ∀x.(p(x) ⇒ ¬q(x)).
hint: Within an assumption p(c), build two separate implications from q(c): one concluding ∃x.(p(x) ∧ q(x)), and the other concluding its negation. Apply Negation Introduction, discharge p(c), and only then generalize c, which must not occur in an active assumption.

prompt: Consider a language with just two object constants - a and b. Given p(a) ⇒ q(b) and p(b) ⇒ q(a), use the Fitch System to prove ∀x.p(x) ⇒ ∀x.q(x).
hint: Assume ∀x.p(x) and use both instances to obtain q(a) and q(b). Apply Domain Closure, citing both instances, before discharging the assumption. Universal Introduction cannot replace Domain Closure here because a and b occur in the premises. fileciteturn0file17turn0file18

prompt: Use the Fitch System to prove ∀x.((p(x) ∨ q(x)) ⇒ (q(x) ∨ p(x))).
hint: Assume p(c) ∨ q(c). Build one implication for each disjunct, both concluding q(c) ∨ p(c), and apply Or Elimination. Discharge the disjunction assumption before applying Universal Introduction to c.

prompt: Given ∀x.∀y.(p(x,y) ⇒ q(y)) and ∃z.¬q(z), use the Fitch System to prove ∀x.¬∀y.p(x,y).
hint: Assume ¬q(d) for the existential subproof. For an arbitrary c, use two separate subproofs with assumption ∀y.p(c,y) to derive q(d) and ¬q(d), respectively. After Negation Introduction, generalize c; discharge the witness assumption before generalizing d and applying Existential Elimination. This follows the chapter’s existential pattern and its restriction on active assumptions for Universal Introduction.

prompt: Use the Fitch System to prove (¬∀x.(p(x) ∧ q(x))) ⇒ ∃x.(¬p(x) ∨ ¬q(x)).
hint: Assume the antecedent, then assume the negation of the existential conclusion. Derive p(c) and q(c) separately by Negation Introduction followed by Negation Elimination. Generalize their conjunction, then use a second subproof to obtain the opposing consequent needed for another application of Negation Introduction. Generalizing c is legitimate only after the assumptions containing c have been discharged.

prompt: Given ∃z.(p(z) ∨ q(z)) and ∀x.(p(x) ⇒ ¬r(x)) and ∀x.(q(x) ⇒ ¬r(x)), use the Fitch System to prove ¬∀x.r(x).
hint: Inside the existential subproof, instantiate both universal implications and apply Or Elimination to obtain ¬r(c). Build two implications with antecedent ∀x.r(x), one concluding r(c) and the other ¬r(c). After Negation Introduction, close the existential subproof using Implication Introduction, Universal Introduction, and Existential Elimination.

prompt: Consider a language with just two object constants - a and b. Given ¬p(a,b) ∧ ¬p(b,a), use the Fitch System to prove ¬∃x.∀y.p(x,y).
hint: For each of a and b, prove that ∀y.p(a,y) or ∀y.p(b,y), respectively, implies the negation of the entire premise conjunction. Use Domain Closure on these two implications, keeping the consequent unchanged. Then an assumed ∃x.∀y.p(x,y) yields the negated conjunction by Existential Elimination; a separate subproof reiterates the conjunction itself. Finish with Negation Introduction. Domain Closure must cite both constant instances.
